title: Analog Electronics One Shot - Chapter 1: Basics

scenes.title: CHAPTER 1: THE BASICS
scenes.subtitle: Current, voltage, resistance and Ohm's law
scenes.narration: Welcome to the complete Analog Electronics one shot. We start from absolute zero. In this first chapter you will see what current, voltage and resistance really are, and why Ohm's law works. Everything else in this course is built on these ideas, so let's make them crystal clear.

Let's zoom inside a copper wire. The grey circles are copper atoms, fixed in place. The small blue dots are free electrons. Each copper atom lets one of its electrons wander freely. Watch them: they are moving fast, but in random directions. Because as many go left as go right, there is no overall flow. So right now, there is no current.

Now we connect a battery across this wire. Look what changes. The electrons still jiggle, but now the whole crowd slowly drifts to the right, toward the positive end. That steady drift of charge is electric current. Notice one important thing: electrons move from negative to positive, but by tradition we draw current from positive to negative. That is called conventional current, and every circuit diagram uses it.

Here is the same idea as a circuit. A twelve volt battery, one hundred ohm resistor, and an ammeter at the bottom. Watch the blue electrons leave the minus terminal, flow through the wire and the resistor, and return to the plus terminal. The ammeter reads one hundred and twenty milliamps. Current is measured in amperes, and one ampere means about six point two quintillion electrons passing a point every second.

So what pushes the electrons? Voltage. Think of voltage as electrical pressure, the push that the battery gives to every electron. Watch the battery value on the left increase from three volts to fifteen volts. See how the electrons speed up, and the ammeter reading climbs with it. More voltage means a stronger push, and a stronger push means more current. Voltage is measured in volts, and it is always measured between two points.

Now let's zoom inside a resistor. Here the atoms are packed more tightly and vibrate more. Watch the electrons: they keep bumping into the atoms, so they drift much more slowly. That opposition to current is resistance. And every bump gives energy to the atoms, which is why a resistor heats up. Resistance is measured in ohms.

Now the most important rule in this chapter: Ohm's law. Watch this graph as we slowly raise the voltage. For the one hundred ohm resistor, the blue line, current rises in a perfectly straight line. For the two hundred ohm resistor, the orange line, it also rises straight, but only half as steeply. Double the voltage, double the current. Double the resistance, half the current. That is Ohm's law: V equals I times R.

Here is Ohm's law written properly. V is the voltage in volts, I is the current in amperes, and R is the resistance in ohms. You can rearrange it whichever way you need. To find current, divide voltage by resistance. To find resistance, divide voltage by current. Remember it as the triangle V over I times R.

scenes.title: SOLVED EXAMPLE 1
scenes.narration: Let's solve a typical exam question. A nine volt battery is connected to a four hundred and fifty ohm resistor. Find the current. Write the formula first: I equals V divided by R. Substitute: nine divided by four hundred and fifty. That gives zero point zero two amperes, which is twenty milliamps. Always convert to milliamps when the answer is small.

Every time current flows through a resistance, energy turns into heat. Watch the resistor glow as current flows. The rate of this energy is power. Power equals voltage times current. Here, twelve volts across twenty four ohms gives half an ampere, so the power is six watts. You can also write power as I squared R, or V squared over R. Resistors have a power rating, and if you exceed it, they burn.

Now two resistors in series, one after another, on a single path. Watch the electrons: there is only one road, so the same current flows through both resistors. The total resistance simply adds up: one hundred plus two hundred is three hundred ohms. So the current is twelve divided by three hundred, forty milliamps. Now look at the green voltmeters. R1 drops four volts and R2 drops eight volts. Together they add up to the full twelve volts of the battery.

scenes.title: SOLVED EXAMPLE 2 · VOLTAGE DIVIDER
scenes.narration: This sharing of voltage in series is called a voltage divider, and it appears in almost every exam. The voltage across R2 equals the supply voltage times R2, divided by the total resistance. Twelve times two hundred, divided by three hundred, gives eight volts. That is exactly what our voltmeter showed. Remember: in series, current is the same, and voltage divides.

Now the same two resistors in parallel, side by side. Watch the electrons: at the top junction, the current splits into two branches and joins again at the bottom. Each resistor gets the full twelve volts. So the one hundred ohm branch carries one hundred and twenty milliamps, and the two hundred ohm branch carries sixty milliamps. The battery supplies their sum, one hundred and eighty milliamps. More current flows through the easier path.

scenes.title: SOLVED EXAMPLE 3 · PARALLEL
scenes.narration: In parallel, the total resistance is found with reciprocals. One over R total equals one over R1 plus one over R2. That is one over one hundred plus one over two hundred, which is three over two hundred. So R total is about sixty six point seven ohms. Notice it is smaller than the smallest resistor. Adding paths in parallel always makes it easier for current to flow. Check it: twelve volts divided by sixty six point seven ohms gives one hundred and eighty milliamps, exactly our total current.

scenes.title: Chapter 1 in one picture
scenes.narration: Let's put chapter one into a single picture. Voltage is the push. It drives current, the flow of charge. Resistance opposes that flow and limits the current. And Ohm's law, V equals I R, ties all three together. In series, the current is the same and voltage divides. In parallel, voltage is the same and current divides.

scenes.title: NEXT: SEMICONDUCTORS
scenes.narration: That completes the basics. In chapter two, we go inside silicon, the material that makes all of electronics possible, and see how adding a tiny impurity turns it into the building block of every diode and transistor.
